prompt: We ran a clean randomized experiment, ~6,000 users per arm, comparing average session length (in minutes). The distribution is a bit right-skewed. I just want to know if the new design increased average session length. Is a t-test fine or do I need something fancier?
response:
Welch's t-test is fine here. With ~6,000 per arm, the CLT has thoroughly done its job — right skew in the raw data barely registers in the sampling distribution of the mean at that n. And since it's a randomized experiment, the difference in means is the unbiased causal estimand by design.

Use Welch's (not Student's) by default — it costs you nothing when variances are equal and protects you if they differ. Don't bother pretesting for equal variances first.

The one thing actually worth reporting: the effect size and a confidence interval on the mean difference in minutes, not just p < 0.05. At n = 6,000 you have a lot of power, so even a trivially small difference will be significant — what matters is whether the increase is large enough to care about.

assertions.text: Says a (Welch) t-test / difference in means is fine here without hedging
Notes that randomization makes the simple difference in means the unbiased causal effect
Notes that the large per-arm n handles the mild skew via the CLT
Does NOT recommend a transformation, GLM, or nonparametric test for this case
Does NOT manufacture unnecessary estimand or robustness caveats; the response is proportionate and largely affirming
